business_fact.fact: We take payments through a Square terminal, so daily item-level sales are available.
We serve roughly 62 dinner covers on a weekday and 110 on Saturday.
The kitchen can push about 15 covers per 15 minutes at peak before tickets back up.
I have owned the restaurant for eight years. Revenue has been flat for the last two.
I am the only one who answers the phone, and I cannot get to it during service.
We are not open for lunch. Dinner service only, 5pm to 10pm, closed Mondays.
We do not take reservations. Saturday is the only night with a real wait.
Tiramisu is currently priced at $7.00 on the dessert menu.
Tiramisu is made in house from my grandmother's recipe. Food cost is about $2.10 per portion.
Average check is $38. Food margin runs 54 percent and labor is 38 percent of revenue.
Tuesday through Thursday are consistently our weakest nights.
Nearest direct competitors are Lucca's one block east and Osteria Bianca three blocks south.
There is a county courthouse two blocks north and a new office building going up on the same street.
We have 14 tables inside and a 20-seat patio that we only use in warm weather.
Break-even is about $2,050 on a normal night.

find.title: "Take one home" — boxed tiramisu offered at every check
find.rationale: The tiramisu is already the item guests write about unprompted, and at least one regular pair is buying two per visit — one eaten in, one boxed — without any prompt from staff (f0f16e7e). Reviews repeatedly call it the best dessert on the street and say it reads as underpriced (4fd96015, d1a6b31f), and local traffic in dessert/late-evening visits is growing while nearby dessert prices have risen ~8% (660be7d3, be2783d5). That means there is unmet demand for the item outside the dine-in dessert course, and it costs $2.10 to make. This is different from the accepted price change and from the 48-hour whole-cake move: it is a to-go single portion, sold at the moment the check drops, to people who have already eaten it and liked it. No new prep, no new labor, no menu redesign — one scripted line from the server ("Want one boxed for tomorrow?") and a stack of containers. At the current $7 (or $9 once you approve the reprice), each boxed portion contributes roughly $4.90–$6.90. Across ~70 covers a night, an attach rate of only 3–4 boxes per service produces the estimate below, and I have deliberately assumed the low end because the ask is new to your staff and depends on them actually saying the line every time.
find.move: Add a single-portion tiramisu to-go, offered by script at every check, at the same price as the dine-in dessert (no price change without your sign-off). I will draft: (1) the one-line server script and the exact moment to say it (when dropping the check, after any dine-in dessert is cleared); (2) a small table tent / check-presenter card reading "Nonna's tiramisu — take one home"; (3) a Square modifier or button labelled "Tiramisu TO GO" so we can count attach rate separately from dine-in dessert. Everything comes to you for OK before it goes live or gets printed. Packaging: use existing to-go containers first; if we need lidded dessert boxes I will price them and ask you before spending anything (staying under the $50 cap). Run it 3 weeks, then read the Square item report for TO GO units per night and per-cover attach rate.

find.title: Voicemail with text callback
find.rationale: Six reviews describe being unable to reach anyone by phone, including one lost large-party booking and one lost whole-cake order. The owner has said they cannot answer during service. A voicemail greeting that invites a text, answered between seatings, converts those calls instead of losing them.
find.move: Record a voicemail greeting directing callers to text, and check it twice per service.

find.title: Turn Saturday turnaways into midweek covers: a walk-away card with a dated Tue–Thu return
find.rationale: Two problems in the memory are the same problem. Saturday at 8pm you are quoting 90 minutes and losing full parties outright — one review says explicitly they left for Lucca's — while Tuesday through Thursday you run near the $2,050 break-even with empty tables. Right now a turned-away party leaves with nothing and their next Italian dinner is somebody else's. A card handed over at the door costs almost nothing and moves that party onto your weakest nights, where the room and the staff are already paid for, so nearly the whole check drops to contribution. No price change, no reservation system, no extra labor at peak — it only asks the host to hand something over at the moment they are already saying no. The comp is one tiramisu per table, food cost about $2.10, and the dessert is the single most-praised item you have, so it is the most persuasive thing you can give away and the cheapest.
find.move:
Draft for your OK: a small card (index-card size, printed cheap or hand-stamped — I'll confirm any print cost with you before spending, and it stays under $50) that reads roughly: "Sorry we couldn't seat you tonight. Come back any Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday in the next 30 days, show this card, and dessert is on Nonna — one tiramisu per table." Write a date and party size on the back when you hand it out.

Execution: keep a stack at the host stand. Every party you turn away or who leaves after being quoted a wait on Friday or Saturday gets one, handed over with the apology, not left in a bowl. Rule for the host: say the line out loud — "we're an hour and a half tonight, but take this and come see us Wednesday, it's quieter and dessert's on us."

Tracking: ring the comped tiramisu as a $0 item on Square (make one button, "Nonna card") so you can count redemptions against cards handed out. Note on a sheet by the phone how many cards you give out each Friday and Saturday. After three weeks you'll have a real redemption rate rather than a guess.

I'll draft the card copy and the host script for your approval; nothing prints or posts without your OK.

find.title: Courthouse & jobsite pre-order lunch box: text or form by 11:15, ready at noon
find.rationale: Lunch service Tue–Thu is now live, but walk-in discovery alone leaves the kitchen idle at exactly the hour when the courthouse two blocks north and the construction/office crowd on the same street are hunting for a seat. Reviews and social chatter are explicit: people work two blocks away, would come twice a week, and are wandering at noon looking for somewhere to eat (bd12de83, 2d73062e, df96a4f5, c7d6937b, a1ebcc27). Local news has covered the incoming daytime worker influx (052f4a72), and lunch competition is intensifying (0e3cebf3), so the offer needs to be easier than walking in. A pre-order lane converts the buyers who only have a 40-minute break and cannot risk a wait: one fixed sheet of 4 pasta/salad boxes at a single price, ordered by text or a free Google Form before 11:15, bagged and paid at the door at noon. It uses dishes already on the lunch line, adds no new prep, needs no phone answered during service (text/form only, which respects the fact that you cannot pick up), and costs under the $50 cap.
find.move: 1) I draft a one-page pre-order card: 4 boxed lunch options built from dishes already on the Tue–Thu lunch line (one pasta, one baked pasta, one chicken/veg plate, one big salad), each with a side and no substitutions, at one flat price you set — you approve the price and the items before anything prints or posts. 2) Ordering channel is text-to-the-restaurant-number or a free Google Form link; cutoff 11:15am, pickup window 11:50–12:20. No phone calls required, so nothing lands on you mid-service. 3) I draft the outreach: 40 printed cards (~$18, under the $50 cap, your OK first) for the courthouse clerk/jury room bulletin board, the two nearest office lobbies, and the construction site trailer, plus a short 'boxed lunches, order by 11:15' line for your Google Business post and Instagram — all drafted, nothing sends without your OK. 4) Kitchen rule: cap pre-orders at 12 boxes per day so dine-in lunch tickets are never delayed; boxes are assembled 11:30–11:50 before the dine-in rush. 5) Track it in Square as its own item so we can count boxes per day and see whether pre-orders are additive or just moving walk-ins.

find.title: Espresso upsell after dessert
find.rationale: Dessert-only and late-evening visits are a growing share of local independent traffic, and the wine list already reads well. Prompting an espresso alongside dessert is a zero-cost add with a high margin.
find.move: Have servers offer espresso with every dessert order.

find.title: Tiramisu → $9
find.rationale: Fourteen separate reviews single out the tiramisu as the best in the city, several explicitly calling it underpriced. The eleven-restaurant survey puts the local average at $10.60 with the nearest rival at $11; Rosa's sits at $7.00 against a $2.10 food cost. Raising to $9 stays below every comparable and leaves the value perception intact.
find.move: Reprice tiramisu from $7.00 to $9.00 and reprint the dessert card.

find.title: Validated parking at the nearby garage
find.rationale: Eight reviews mention parking difficulty, consistently paired with praise for the food — diners are arriving despite it rather than being turned away by it. No new public capacity is planned. A validation deal would improve the experience but the evidence does not support a large revenue effect, and the cost sits against the owner's monthly cap.
find.move: Approach the garage two doors down about a validation rate for diners.

find.title: Make the phone answer itself: voicemail script + Google auto-reply for the questions people actually call about
find.rationale: Rosa's loses guests at the exact moment they are trying to choose it. Reviews show people calling or posting to ask basic things — whether there is midday service, how long the Saturday wait really is — and getting nothing (a1ebcc27, 7a966947, f82c0037). One party said an hour-and-a-half quote sent them to Lucca's instead (96d0ae93); another abandoned after two Saturdays of no straight answer. The owner is the only person on the phone and cannot pick up during service, so every one of those calls is a silent turnaway. This is fixable without touching prices, staffing, or reservations: a written voicemail greeting and a Google Business Profile auto-reply that state hours (including the new Tue–Thu lunch), that walk-ins are seated first-come, the honest typical Saturday wait by time slot, and the suggestion to arrive before 6:30 or after 8:45. Guests who now hang up and go a block east instead get a reason to come at a time Rosa's can actually seat them. Cost is zero, so it sits under the $50 cap, and nothing goes live until the owner reads and approves the exact wording. Conservatively this recovers roughly one to two covers per day at a $38 average check, which is why the number is small and deliberately beatable rather than a headline.
find.move: Draft, for the owner's approval only, two pieces of copy: (1) a 25-second voicemail greeting for the restaurant line stating dinner hours Tue–Sun 5–10pm, closed Monday, new Tue–Thu lunch, walk-ins only, typical Saturday wait by arrival time, and the best low-wait windows; (2) a Google Business Profile / messages auto-reply with the same facts plus a one-line link to the menu. Owner records the greeting and pastes the auto-reply once approved. Update the Saturday wait figures monthly from Square covers data. No spend, no price changes, nothing published before owner sign-off.

find.title: Tuesday–Thursday three-course set menu
find.rationale: The owner reports Tuesday through Thursday as consistently weakest, with four of eleven nearby restaurants now running midweek promotions and one direct rival at a $45 prix fixe. A set menu at a lower price point fills seats that are otherwise empty, at controlled food cost.
find.move: Design a three-course midweek set menu and price it against the rival's $45.

find.title: Price the tiramisu to match its reputation ($7 → $9, owner approves first)
find.rationale: Tiramisu is the single most praised item on the menu and reviewers explicitly say it is underpriced — one says they would pay double, another notes it is the best thing on the menu yet the cheapest dessert offered, and repeat guests order two per visit. Broader review sentiment says the whole menu reads as underpriced, and nearby comparable restaurants have raised average dessert prices about 8% since spring, so $9 stays in line with the street. At $2.10 food cost, a $2 increase is nearly pure margin: no new labor, no new prep, no spend. With the late dessert window already live, dessert volume is the easiest lever left that does not touch the kitchen's 15-covers-per-15-minutes ceiling. Conservative math: roughly 75 covers on an average open day, assume only ~12 tiramisus sold, allow for a few guests trading down, and count about $1.60 net per portion — that lands near $19/day, so I am predicting 1500c to leave room for attrition. Prices are not changed until you say yes, per your rule.
find.move: I will draft a one-page price-change note for your approval: raise tiramisu from $7.00 to $9.00 on the dessert menu, effective the Tuesday after you approve. Deliverables I prepare and you sign off on before anything goes live: (1) the reprinted dessert section with tiramisu listed as 'Nonna's Tiramisu — made in house from my grandmother's recipe, $9', since the story justifies the number; (2) a one-line script for servers when they clear mains ('the tiramisu is made here from Rosa's grandmother's recipe — it's the one thing people come back for'); (3) a Square tracking sheet comparing tiramisu units and total dessert dollars for the 14 days before versus the 14 days after, so we can see if units drop faster than dollars rise. No other prices change. Zero spend. If units fall more than 25% over two weeks, we revert to $7 and I say so plainly.

find.title: Reply to every recent low review
find.rationale: The one and two star reviews cluster almost entirely on Saturday waits and unanswered phone calls — both now addressed. Replying to each one publicly, naming the fix, converts the strongest objection a prospective diner will read into evidence that the place listens.
find.move: Draft a reply to each one and two star review from the last ninety days for the owner to approve.

find.title: Make the new lunch service findable: fix Google and site hours, post the lunch menu
find.rationale: Lunch service is already live Tue–Thu, but the outside world still says 'dinner only.' People are literally asking online whether Rosa's is open midday and saying the website says dinner, and multiple reviewers say they work two blocks away and would come at noon if they knew. That is demand that already exists being lost to stale listings, not to competitors. Fixing the Google Business Profile hours, adding a lunch menu section and a weekly Post, and putting a hand-lettered 'Now open for lunch Tue–Thu' card in the window costs nothing but attention, and it is the cheapest way to raise the ceiling on a service the kitchen is already staffing. Also worth noting competition for the daytime office and courthouse crowd is intensifying, so being invisible at noon is expensive.
find.move: Draft (for owner approval, nothing published until OK'd): 1) Google Business Profile edits — change hours to show Tue–Thu 11:30am–2pm lunch plus 5–10pm dinner, closed Mondays; upload 3 photos of lunch plates; add the lunch menu as a menu section with prices unchanged. 2) One Google Post: 'Now open for lunch, Tuesday to Thursday, 11:30–2. Same kitchen, same pasta, out the door in 45 minutes.' 3) Same three lines added to the website header and the top of the Yelp/Facebook about text. 4) Update the voicemail greeting already in place to state lunch hours in the first sentence. 5) One printed 8x10 window card and a table tent for dinner guests reading 'We now serve lunch Tue–Thu 11:30–2' — printing under $20, inside the $50 cap. No price changes anywhere.

find.title: Take midweek group bookings only: a Tue–Thu table for 6+ that the courthouse and nearby offices can actually reserve
find.rationale: Tue–Thu are the weakest nights and the no-reservation policy quietly turns away the one segment that cannot walk in on spec: work groups of 6–12 from the courthouse two blocks north and the law/office tenants on the street. Four of eleven comparable restaurants are already advertising midweek offers, and interest in set menus is up, so an organized group is currently going to a competitor that will simply hold a table. Accepting reservations for parties of 6+ on Tue/Wed/Thu only changes nothing about Saturday policy, costs no ad spend, and fills seats on nights that already run below the $2,050 break-even. Because the owner cannot answer the phone during service, bookings come in by a form/email/voicemail with a written-back confirmation, not by live call. Capped at one group per night, seated at 6:00 or 6:30, so the 15-covers-per-15-minutes kitchen ceiling is never tested. Conservative because it is a new channel with a ramp: the estimate assumes roughly one party of six to eight per week and that a portion would have visited anyway.
find.move: 1) Draft (for owner OK) a one-page 'Midweek group table' sheet: parties of 6–12, Tuesday/Wednesday/Thursday only, seating at 6:00pm or 6:30pm, one group per night, choice of the existing three-course set menu already on the line, no deposit, confirm by email. 2) Add a single booking path the owner can handle off-service: a free Google Form (or a request-a-table email link) on the site and Google profile, plus a voicemail line in the outgoing greeting — 'for parties of six or more Tuesday to Thursday, leave your name, night, and party size and I will text you back tonight.' Owner replies once daily after 10pm with a confirm/decline text. 3) Distribution, zero paid media: print 40 copies (under the $50 cap, exact cost to be confirmed first) and hand-deliver to the courthouse clerk's office and bar association board, the two nearest law firms, and the site office/GC trailer for the new building; ask each for the office manager's email and send the same sheet as a PDF. 4) On the floor, tape a small note in the server station: any Tue–Thu table of 6+ that mentions a work group gets the sheet with the check. 5) Track in Square by tagging group checks with a note; review after 30 days on three numbers — number of groups booked, covers per group, average check versus the $38 baseline.

find.title: Whole tiramisu to order, 48 hours ahead
find.rationale: A customer tried to order a whole tiramisu for a birthday, could not reach anyone, and gave up — that is a named lost sale, not an inference. Fourteen reviews single the dessert out as the best in the city, and local search for tiramisu peaks in the evening. Food cost is $2.10 a portion, so a whole cake sold at $48 carries an unusually high margin and uses prep and skill that already exist. Small, but it costs nothing to try.
find.move: Offer whole tiramisu at $48 with 48 hours notice, taken by text, and add a line to the dessert card.

find.title: Sell the empty 5:00–6:15 hour: a held "first seating" on Friday and Saturday, booked by text
find.rationale: Weekend demand in the district spikes between 7pm and 8:30pm (9129f715), and Rosa's is turning parties away at 8pm with 90-minute quotes (96d0ae93, 7a966947, f82c0037) while the 5:00–6:15 window on those same nights runs soft. Guests are already self-selecting into early dinners here — one review says they came early specifically because there is no lunch, and would come at noon if there were (2d73062e) — and district diners increasingly abandon a restaurant purely over the wait (0cff7b41). The doorway crush is a known complaint (cf77baf6). Holding a small number of early tables does three things at once: it books revenue in an hour that currently sells nothing, it moves some peak-hour parties out of the 7pm crush, and it gives the room a clean second turn before peak. It requires no new spend and rides the text-ahead waitlist you already have live (55a0de17), so it never touches the phone during service. This is deliberately not open reservations — it is 5 tables, early slot only, released to walk-ins after 10 minutes.
find.move: Draft for your approval: hold 5 of the 14 inside tables for a "first seating" at 5:00 and 5:15 on Friday and Saturday only. Guests claim a slot through the same text-ahead number the Saturday waitlist already uses — they text a name, party size, and time, and get back a one-line confirmation plus "we hold the table 10 minutes." After 10 minutes the table goes to walk-ins. I will write: (1) the confirmation and release text templates, (2) a Google Business Profile post and a line for the front window/menu — "First seating 5:00 & 5:15, Fri & Sat — text to hold a table, no wait," (3) a one-page sheet for the host stand covering how to log holds and when to release them. Nothing publishes until you OK the wording. No spend. Track it in Square by counting covers seated before 6:15 on Fri/Sat against the four weeks prior, and watch whether 8pm turnaways drop.

find.title: Second server on Friday and Saturday peak
find.rationale: Six reviews describe one server covering the entire floor, and the complaints are about pace rather than warmth — the same reviews praise the staff. Local diners increasingly abandon a restaurant over wait time. Saturday runs 110 covers against a kitchen that pushes fifteen per fifteen minutes, so the constraint is front of house, not the line. A second server for the 6pm to 9pm block costs roughly $51 a day averaged across the week; the prediction is net of that.
find.move: Add a second floor server for the 6pm to 9pm block on Friday and Saturday.

find.title: Late dessert window, 9pm to 10pm
find.rationale: Dessert and late-evening visits are a growing share of local traffic, and weekend demand peaks sharply at 7pm to 8:30pm — leaving the last hour underused with the kitchen already staffed. A dessert-and-drink-only window monetises seats that would otherwise turn over empty.
find.move: Advertise a dessert-and-drinks-only window for the last hour of service.

find.title: Sell the empty Saturday 5–6:15 window instead of losing the 8pm turnaways
find.rationale: Saturday demand piles into 7:00–8:30pm while the room is soft at 5:00–6:15, and the kitchen ceiling (15 covers/15 min) means peak demand cannot be served no matter what. Reviews show people are being quoted 60–90 minutes and walking to Lucca's, and others nearly left mid-wait. You cannot add peak capacity, but you can move demand into the hour you already have staffed and empty. This needs no price change, no reservation book, no phone answering during service, and no spend — just a written promise that arriving before 6:15 on Saturday means walking straight in. Filling the shoulder also relieves the 7pm crush slightly, since some parties that would have queued at 7:15 come at 6.
find.move: Draft (for your OK, nothing published without it) a three-part 'Saturday, no wait before 6:15' push: (1) a Google Business Profile post and one Instagram/Facebook post saying 'Saturdays at Rosa's: walk in before 6:15pm and we seat you right away. After 7pm, expect a wait.' (2) A half-page card printed on your own printer, one per table Tue–Fri and taped inside the front window, with the same line — so the regulars who currently show up at 7:45 self-select earlier. (3) Update your voicemail greeting to the same sentence so the calls you cannot answer during service still get the answer they want. Zero spend beyond paper. Measurement: in Square, pull Saturday covers in the 5:00–6:30 window for the four Saturdays before and the four after, plus total Saturday covers; success is total Saturday covers up, not just redistributed.

find.title: Open the patio every warm night
find.rationale: Six reviews mention the patio, three of them describing it closed on a night that would have suited it. Local search interest in patio dining is up thirty four percent and the forecast holds twenty two consecutive evenings above sixty five degrees. Twenty additional seats at 54 percent food margin, with no new labour if set up before service.
find.move: Set the patio before service on any evening forecast above sixty five degrees.

find.title: Raise pasta mains by $2
find.rationale: Seven separate reviews describe the prices as low — two of them unprompted, one saying outright that the bill comes in lower than expected. Osteria Bianca runs $24 to $32 against Rosa's $18 to $24, and Trattoria Nona raised its mains two dollars across the board this month with no visible complaint. Average dessert prices in the area are already up eight percent since spring. At roughly 38 pasta covers a night a two dollar rise carries almost entirely to margin. Owner rule requires approval before any price change, so this stays a proposal.
find.move: Raise pasta mains by $2.00 across the board and reprint the dinner menu.

find.title: Lunch service, Tuesday to Thursday
find.rationale: Ten separate observations show unmet midday demand around the courthouse, including a forum thread where nine people gave up and ate at their desks. Nine of eleven nearby Italian restaurants already serve lunch; Rosa's is one of the two that do not. A nine-storey office confirmed for September occupancy adds roughly four hundred daytime workers within two blocks. This is the largest single opportunity in the corpus.
find.move: Build a limited lunch menu from existing prep and open Tuesday to Thursday, 11am to 2pm, before the office opens in September.

find.title: Text-ahead waitlist for Saturdays
find.rationale: Twelve reviews describe abandoning or nearly abandoning a Saturday visit, and several name the absence of a waitlist specifically. Two of the three nearest rivals now advertise text-ahead or reservations. At 110 Saturday covers and a $38 average check, recovering even a handful of walkaways per night pays for itself immediately.
find.move: Stand up a text-when-ready waitlist for Saturday service and put a sign on the door.
